I have found that patients are sometimes reluctant to tell doctors if they are using alternative therapy and in some instances it can interact with their medications. An example is St John's Wort which thins the blood, this can cause major issues if a patient has surgery and doesn't tell their doctor. Doctors need to work harder at making their patients feel comfortable about telling them about any alternative therapy they might be using, while balancing not endorsing anything that may cause harm.

I think many doctors are resistant to consider alternative therapy practitioners as colleagues because many disciplines lack a registration process or minimum standard to be considered a practitioner. Many 'treatments' are not supported by evidence and would be better accepted if they had a results of large scale randomized control trial available and published. If alternative therapists worked together to professionalize their disciplines doctors would take them a lot more seriously.

One hospital I worked in trialed pharmacists meeting with patients prior to chemotherapy and discussing any medications or alternative therapy they might ingest. They then researched all interactions with the planned treatment and met with the patient and explained what all the evidence means. This was highly successful and the majority of patients took the pharmacists advice. I think this project was a good balance because it gave patients the opportunity to tell staff about alternative therapies they were using and provided them with evidence based advice.
